title: Building Production RAG Systems
summary: The execution path from a working retrieval demo to something that survives real traffic and real documents.
overview: Most RAG tutorials stop at 'retrieve and generate.' Production RAG is mostly the parts that come after that: evaluation, guardrails, and handling the documents that don't fit your assumptions.
problem: A RAG demo that works on ten clean PDFs usually breaks on a real document corpus — inconsistent formatting, duplicate content, and documents that contradict each other.
prerequisites: A working embeddings + vector store setup; familiarity with the tradeoffs in the Chunking Strategies knowledge article.
recommendedStack: A vector store with metadata filtering (Qdrant or pgvector), a reranker, and a generation model with a context window large enough to hold reranked results comfortably.
commonMistakes: Treating retrieval and generation quality as one metric — a system can generate fluent, well-cited answers from the wrong retrieved chunk, and that failure is invisible unless retrieval is evaluated separately.
tradeoffs: Reranking adds latency for a precision gain; skipping it only makes sense once you've measured that your base retrieval precision is already high enough for your domain.

steps.title: Establish a retrieval-only evaluation set
steps.detail: Before touching generation quality, build a set of queries with known-correct source chunks, so retrieval precision can be measured independently of how fluent the final answer sounds.

steps.title: Pick a chunking strategy deliberately
steps.detail: Match the strategy to your corpus's actual structure — see the Chunking Strategies knowledge article for the concrete tradeoff.

steps.title: Add reranking once retrieval precision plateaus
steps.detail: Rerankers help most when the vector store's raw top-k is noisy; measure before adding the latency cost.

steps.title: Add a citation check before shipping
steps.detail: Verify generated citations actually correspond to retrieved chunks — this is what catches silent retrieval failure, per the Enterprise RAG Architecture page.

steps.title: Re-run the retrieval eval after every corpus change
steps.detail: Document corpus changes are the most common cause of retrieval regressions that generation-level evals won't catch.

body.raw: Building a RAG demo and building a RAG system that survives production traffic are different jobs. This playbook is the second one — the execution path, not the concept explanation (that's what the Knowledge base entries are for).
